name: Amber
spiritual: Carries the memory of ancient forests
physical: Traditionally worn by babies and adults as a folk comfort
Crystal healers link it to throat and neck comfort
Associated with a feeling of vitality
summary: Amber is fossilised tree resin millions of years old, warm to the touch and rich in folklore, used for vitality, joy, protection and gentle comfort.
intro: Amber is not a mineral but fossilised tree resin, hardened over tens of millions of years into a warm, glowing gem. Colours run from pale lemon to deep cognac, and occasionally rare shades of green, blue or red. It is astonishingly light, feels warm against the skin and gives off a faint pine scent when rubbed or warmed. Many pieces hold treasures: tiny insects, leaves, pollen and air bubbles frozen in time. When rubbed on cloth, it picks up a static charge, a trick known since antiquity. Because it is so soft, it is carved into beads, pendants and cabochons rather than faceted, and has been prized in jewellery for thousands of years.
history: Amber has been treasured since the Stone Age, with carved amber beads found in graves across northern Europe. The Greek word for amber, elektron, gave us the word electricity after Thales of Miletus noticed its static charge. The Roman writer Pliny recorded the Amber Road, a trade route carrying Baltic amber to the Mediterranean, and Nero is said to have sent an expedition to find it. In the seventeenth century, the Teutonic Knights controlled the amber trade, and the famous Amber Room, built for Prussian and Russian royalty, was a wonder of its age. Folk traditions across Europe valued amber as a charm against evil, and Baltic communities still make amber teething necklaces, a folk custom without proven medical benefit.
meaning: Amber is the sun in stone form, a warm, comforting gem associated with vitality, optimism and protection. Practitioners connect it to the Solar Plexus and Sacral chakras, saying it lifts a heavy mood and restores a sense of personal warmth. Because it was once a living tree resin, it is regarded as a stone of life energy and ancient memory, holding the sense of deep time. It is said to absorb negative energy and transmute it into something gentler, which is why many people wear it as a protective talisman. In folk belief, amber is also linked to throat comfort and to well-being in general, though these are traditional ideas and not medical claims. It remains a favourite for people who like warm, grounded stones with deep history.
howToUse: Wear an amber necklace or bracelet against the skin, where body warmth brings out its scent and glow. Hold a polished piece while meditating on sunlight and growth. Keep a raw chunk on a windowsill out of direct sun as a decorative focal point, or on a desk to lift your mood. Burn nothing; amber is flammable. In a grid, place it in the south for warmth. Pair with citrine for a sunny abundance layout. Remember that amber is fragile, so store it carefully.
care: Amber is very soft and sensitive to heat, solvents, perfume and hairspray. Never soak it or use chemical cleaners. Wipe with a soft damp cloth and dry it, and polish gently with a soft cloth. Cleanse it with sound, smoke or moonlight, or a rest on a selenite plate; avoid direct sunlight for long periods, as it can darken and crack the resin. Store it away from heat, in a soft pouch, apart from harder stones. Put on jewellery after perfume or hairspray, not before.
identify: Real amber is light, feels warm, and floats in a saturated salt solution (about one part salt to four parts water), while most plastics and glass sink. A hot needle on a hidden spot gives a pine-like scent in real amber, and a chemical odour in plastic. Real amber static-charges when rubbed. Copal, younger resin, becomes sticky with a drop of acetone; amber does not. Pressed amber (ambroid) and reconstituted pieces exist, and many are heat treated or dyed.

faq.a: No. Amber is fossilised tree resin, an organic gem with no crystal structure. It is still part of the crystal tradition because of its beauty, age and long history of use as a protective stone.

faq.q: How can I tell if amber is real?
faq.a: Real amber is lightweight, feels warm, floats in saltwater, and gives a faint pine scent when gently warmed. Plastic and glass sink, and copal sticks to acetone. A trusted seller or lab is the safest check.
Brief contact is fine, but never soak it or use chemicals, perfume or hot water, as it is soft and can dull or crack. Wipe with a soft slightly damp cloth, then dry it.
